Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Setup 3 Tricks 4 Scoring 5 Variants 5.1 Initial points 5.2 Rule set 5.3 Jack of Diamonds bonus 5.4 Penalty card play limit 5.5 Face value scoring 5.6 High Spades scoring 5.7 Starter card 5.8 Shooting the moon 5.9 Pass cycle 5.10 Skip uneventful final tricks Overview Hearts is a card game for 4 players, every player for themselves. It uses the standard 52-card pack, ranked A (high) to 2 (low), with the figure cards being K Q J high to low. Setup The entire deck is dealt, giving each player a hand of 13 cards. After looking at your hand, choose three cards to pass to another player. The passing rotation is: (1st hand) to the player on your left, (2nd hand) to the player on your right, (3rd hand) to the player across the table, (4th hand) no passing. The rotation repeats until the game ends. Tricks After passing cards, the player holding the 2♣ leads the first trick. Each player must follow suit if possible. If you have no cards of the suit led, you may play a card of any suit. Exception: You may not play a ​♥ or the Q♠ on the first trick, even if you have no clubs. The highest card of the suit led wins the trick. The winner of a trick starts the next trick. Hearts may not be led until a ​♥ has been played (this is called "breaking hearts"). There is no trump suit. Scoring At the end of each hand, each ​♥ taken by a player counts -1, and the Q♠ counts -13. If one player has taken all 13 ​♥ s and Q♠ (this is known as "shooting the moon", or "slam"), that player scores 0 and all other players score -26. Warning other players about an attempt to shoot the moon is team play, and a breach of Hearts etiquette. When one or more players reach zero, the game ends. The player with the highest score wins. Variants Initial points Start with 50 points Start with 75 points Start with 100 points Rule set Hearts Omnibus Hearts: J♦ is +10 Black Maria: A♠ is -7, K♠ is -10, no penalty card play limit, always pass right, no shooting the moon, player left of dealer always starts Spot Hearts: A♥ is -14, K♥ is -13, Q♥ is -12, J♥ is -11, and other ​♥ are negative their face value Custom Jack of Diamonds bonus Disabled Enabled ( J♦ worth +10) Penalty card play limit Default (no points on first trick, cannot lead ​♥ until they break) Points in the first trick (cannot lead ​♥ until they break) Disabled Face value scoring Disabled [Meaning??] Enabled [Meaning??] High Spades scoring Disabled This would be the standard game. Q♠ is -13. The other Spades have no points. Enabled In addition to Q♠ being -13, these negative points are also added: A♠ is -7, K♠ is -10. Starter card Enabled ( 2♣ always starts) Disabled (player left of dealer always starts) Shooting the moon Default (other players receive -26 points) Positive moon scoring (player receives +26 points) Disabled [Meaning?? Does this mean Shooting the moon will not apply?] Pass cycle Default Remove no pass hands Always pass right Skip uneventful final tricks Yes No

[Rating: 1/10] Well, I do like it a lot. Until someone is plotting to shoot the moon, then it's painfully obvious, how they spend a long time to carefully plan out all their future moves. Ughhh, I swear it's the [i]slowest[/i] trick-taking game I ever played because of that.  There's something about the queen of spades being so valuable that provides a nice structure to rounds, it becomes all about that. But it overshadows the hearts, so why even call it Hearts anymore? There's something about trick-avoidance that gets tiring, like everyone's passive-aggressively mean, nobody's controlling much. It's like...

[Rating: 2/10] Trick-taking without bidding makes for an unsatisfying exercise in playing the odds.  Give me Spades.  Heck, I'd even rather play Euchre.

[Rating: 2/10] The game I would not play even if there was nothing else. The computer version is bad enough, but playing it with people is the equivalent of four impacted wisdom teeth.

[Rating: 2/10] rated to high.  In fact people who rate it high need to get out and check some good games.... get some perspective

[Rating: 2.5/10] Just too simple. Simple to the point of boring. It's better than Whist, but that's not saying a lot. I'm glad I tried it once.

[Rating: 3/10] I like Spades a lot better, but this is the game that brought me into the gaming hobby, so I've got to give it credit.

[Rating: 3/10] I find that I am not a big fan of Hearts (being one who prefers to take tricks rather than duck them).

[Rating: 3/10] When with non-BGG's or normaly at my parents or dull friends or family house this maybe come up!! Poor souls almost only know this kind of games. Makes me want to sleep instead.

[Rating: 3/10] Very light card game, but interesting none the less.  IMHO not much fun against MSFT computer opponents.  They suck too bad. I'd rather play almost any game though.

[Rating: 3/10] Probably the best introductory trick-taking card game, but it isn't very deep. Once you're familiar with the rules, the game "plays itself". The Chinese version is more interesting. Spades beats Hearts too.  My relatives play this Chinese version ('Roll the Pig'), which doesn't add much...  - 2-5 of Hearts do not give any points, J/Q/K/A of Hearts are +20/30/40/50 points - Queen of Spades ('Pig') is +130 points - Jack of Diamonds ('Goat') is -10 points - 10 of Clubs doubles your points (including if it's negative)  2+1
